plan.topic: Mounjaro vs Zepbound: same medicine (tirzepatide), different US-approved uses, labels and device options
plan.angle: Same structure. Chapter 2 quotes each US PI's Section 1 indications word for word, including Mounjaro's pediatric (10+ years, T2D) indication and any cardiovascular risk-reduction indication if the 27 Aug 2026 PI lists it, plus Zepbound's chronic weight management and OSA populations exactly as printed. Name the trial programme behind each (SURPASS / SURPASS-PEDS; SURMOUNT; SURMOUNT-OSA), each with its full population. State plainly: 'In the US, Mounjaro's label is for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound's label is for weight management and obstructive sleep apnea, in the populations listed.' Chapter 5 lists only the device options printed in each PI's Dosage Forms/How Supplied section (e.g. Zepbound: single-dose pen, single-dose vial, KwikPen per the current label), with each IFU cited at its own verified URL and no amounts. Chapter 3 keeps 'different trial populations, so the tables can't be compared head to head.' Keep all the other rules (no cost, dosing, switching), the don't-switch/stop/change line, one GI line ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'), 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line, and the closing line.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide: Mounjaro vs Zepbound, What's Different?
plan.why: Playbook L2. A broad, search-demand question with steady demand ('is mounjaro the same as zepbound'), with the ObesityWeek Zepbound push as a hook. Every claim can be checked against the two US labels, so it should pass fact-check. | fact-check: Good evergreen, high-search explainer and safe if it stays label-only. Three accuracy risks in the angle as written. (1) The Mounjaro indication is no longer just 'type 2 diabetes in adults'. FDA has since approved Mounjaro as an adjunct to diet and exercise for glycemic control in pediatric patients 10 years and older with T2D (SURPASS-PEDS; see FDA letter https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2025/215866Orig1s039ltr.pdf). Lilly has also announced a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication for adults with T2D. Paraphrasing or shortening the indication from memory would be wrong, so copy Section 1 of the 27 Aug 2026 PI word for word, including every population and age. The same goes for Zepbound Section 1 (28 Aug 2026): copy any age or population wording exactly rather than assuming 'adults' for every indication. (2) Device list: FDA approved a 4-dose single-patient-use Zepbound KwikPen in the US on 23 Feb 2026. Take the US device options for each brand only from Section 3/16 of each PI and its own IFU URLs. Don't assume Mounjaro has a US KwikPen, and don't leave out the Mounjaro single-dose vial if the PI lists one. Each IFU needs its own URL (e.g. https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-pen-us-ifu.pdf). Never cite the PI page or a PI anchor as the IFU. (3) Chapter 2 must not imply Mounjaro is used or approved for weight loss in the US. Only say what the label says. Chapter 6 (UK/AU) is fine if it's one factual line sourced to the MHRA/TGA product information, with no market talk. Packaging note: '▶ Watch next' is a publisher instruction only. It must never appear as placeholder text in the description.

package.pinned_comment: Mounjaro and Zepbound are the same medicine, tirzepatide, under two different US labels for different approved uses. Outside the US it can differ: in the EU, Mounjaro's authorisation covers both type 2 diabetes and weight management. Save this for your next appointment. Don't switch between Mounjaro and Zepbound on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide: Mounjaro vs Zepbound, What's Different?
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim plus a one-sentence open loop: 'Same medicine' is the short answer by 10 s, the US-label split is the second payoff by about 25 s, and the open loop is the KwikPen, a device option both brands share that many people haven't heard of, paid off in the device chapter

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide is in both Mounjaro and Zepbound, so what's actually different for you?

visual.stock_query: curious person holding two pen boxes

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: the viewer's exact search question, drug first, as the first line

scenes.narration: Short answer: it's the same medicine. Both are tirzepatide, both are made by Eli Lilly, and both are once-weekly injections under the skin.
What's different is the US label. That means who each one is approved for, and the trials behind it. And the devices? That part might surprise you.

visual.stock_query: two label documents side by side

scenes.retention_device: Promise: concrete differences to come, plus a device tease

scenes.narration: Here's the first one, in plain words. In the US, Mounjaro's label is for type 2 diabetes, including lowering heart risk in some adults with it, and Zepbound's label is for weight management and obstructive sleep apnea, in the populations listed.

visual.stock_query: split screen, two labelled pen boxes

scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff at about 20–25 s

scenes.narration: And stay for the device chapter, because both of these brands come in a form a lot of people haven't heard of.

visual.stock_query: mystery gift box with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Open loop (one sentence), paid off in the device chapter

scenes.narration: Picture someone we'll call Dana, 52. She's at the pharmacy counter collecting her Zepbound, and the label on the bag says tirzepatide.
scenes.retention_device: Hypothetical 'you' scenario begins the relatable thread

scenes.narration: That weekend at dinner, her brother says, 'I'm on Mounjaro. Same thing, right?' And Dana suddenly wonders if one of them has the wrong medicine.

visual.stock_query: siblings talking at family dinner table

scenes.narration: If you've felt that little jolt of confusion, you're not alone. Two brand names for one molecule is genuinely confusing, and asking about it is the smart move.
So let's read the two US labels the way a pharmacist would, section by section, and see exactly where they split.

visual.stock_query: friendly pharmacist opening a label booklet

scenes.retention_device: Roadmap in one line before the chapter change

scenes.narration: So who is each one actually approved for?

visual.stock_query: chapter card, two labels, question mark

scenes.narration: In every US prescribing label, the first numbered section is Section 1, Indications and Usage. Think of it as the official guest list: the people a medicine is approved to treat.

visual.stock_query: guest list clipboard at a door

scenes.retention_device: Analogy to make a dry term memorable

scenes.narration: Mounjaro's Section 1 lists two uses. One: alongside diet and exercise, to improve blood sugar control in people with type 2 diabetes. Two: to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.

items: Use 1: blood sugar control, type 2 diabetes
Use 2: lower heart attack, stroke, CV death risk
Use 2 population: high-risk adults with type 2 diabetes
visual.stock_query: blood sugar meter beside heart icon

scenes.retention_device: First half of the comparison, with a second use many don't know

scenes.narration: And it isn't only adults. The FDA has approved Mounjaro's blood sugar use in children aged 10 and older with type 2 diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Mounjaro: ages 10 and up, type 2 diabetes

scenes.retention_device: Surprising detail most viewers don't know

scenes.narration: Mounjaro's label also has its own warnings section. We'll get to the warnings both labels share in a minute.

items: Shared warnings: later in this video

scenes.retention_device: Signpost that plants a later payoff

scenes.narration: Now notice what isn't on Mounjaro's guest list. Its US Section 1 doesn't list weight management.
scenes.on_screen_text: US Mounjaro: no weight use listed

visual.myth: Mounjaro is US-approved for weight loss
visual.fact: Its US label lists type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: Zepbound's Section 1 has two uses. Both are alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity.

visual.stock_query: Zepbound box with two highlighted lines

scenes.retention_device: Count-based tease for the next two scenes

scenes.narration: Use one: to reduce excess body weight and keep it off long term, in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related condition.
Use two: to treat moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.
Zepbound's label also notes that it contains tirzepatide, and that using it together with other tirzepatide products or other GLP-1 medicines isn't recommended.

visual.stock_query: calm mascot beside two pens, no stacking

scenes.retention_device: Practical safety point that answers Dana's worry

scenes.narration: Which answers Dana's dinner-table moment. She and her brother are on the same molecule, under two different US labels, for different approved uses.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the first loop, returns to the thread

scenes.narration: Labels do get updated, so the current Section 1 is always the final word. But a label is only as strong as the trials behind it, and that's where it gets interesting.

visual.stock_query: label lifting to reveal trial charts

scenes.narration: Where did those two guest lists come from?
scenes.on_screen_text: Where did the labels come from?

scenes.narration: Mounjaro's blood sugar use rests on the SURPASS trial programme, run in adults with type 2 diabetes. Its heart-risk use comes from SURPASS-CVOT, in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
scenes.retention_device: Naming the programmes anchors the label

scenes.narration: Take SURPASS-1. Adults with type 2 diabetes managed with diet and exercise alone took tirzepatide or a placebo for 40 weeks.
HbA1c, the roughly three-month blood sugar average, fell by about one point nine to two point one percentage points across the three tirzepatide doses. On placebo, it barely moved.
The children's indication comes from SURPASS-PEDS, a trial in young people with type 2 diabetes, aged 10 to 17.

visual.stock_query: teen and parent talking with doctor

scenes.narration: Zepbound's weight label rests on SURMOUNT. SURMOUNT-1 enrolled 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Big number to humanise the trial

scenes.narration: Over 72 weeks, average weight change on tirzepatide ranged from about 15 to 21 percent, depending on dose. On placebo, it was three point one percent.
And the sleep apnea use? That came from a completely different pair of trials.

SURMOUNT-OSA ran two 52-week trials in adults with obesity and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. One enrolled people not using a breathing machine like CPAP. The other enrolled people who were.

visual.stock_query: bedroom with and without CPAP machine

scenes.retention_device: Clever trial design as a micro-story

scenes.narration: The main measure was breathing interruptions per hour of sleep. In the trial without a machine, they fell by about 25 an hour on tirzepatide, versus about 5 on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Breathing events per hour, trial 1, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: In the trial with a machine, the drop was about 29 an hour on tirzepatide. On placebo, it was about five and a half.

visual.stat_label: Breathing events per hour, trial 2, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: Same molecule in every one of these trials. But very different people, and that matters a lot for what comes next.
So why does Zepbound's side-effect table look so different from Mounjaro's?
Flip to Section 6 of each label and the percentages don't line up. That can feel unsettling, as if one brand is harsher than the other.
scenes.retention_device: Name a worry the viewer may share

scenes.narration: But each table comes from its own trial pool. Mounjaro's comes from adults with type 2 diabetes. Zepbound's comes from weight-management trials: one that excluded type 2 diabetes, and one that enrolled only people with it.
Different trial populations, so the tables can't be compared head to head.
Here's a real example: acute pancreatitis, a rare but serious inflammation of the pancreas.
In Mounjaro's diabetes trials, it was reported at zero point two three people per 100 years of exposure. In the comparator groups, zero point one one.

visual.stat_label: Per 100 years, Mounjaro diabetes trials vs comparators

scenes.narration: In Zepbound's weight trials, it was zero point one four on tirzepatide, versus zero point one five on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Per 100 years, Zepbound weight trials vs placebo

scenes.narration: Same molecule, different numbers. The people, the comparators and the trial designs all differed, so each table is read on its own terms.
Stomach side effects like nausea and diarrhea were the most common in both labels. In the Zepbound label, they happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.
One more from the Zepbound weight trials. Hair loss was reported in five point four percent of people on tirzepatide. On placebo, zero point nine percent.

visual.stat_label: Hair loss, Zepbound weight trials vs placebo

scenes.retention_device: Relatable stat many viewers search for

scenes.narration: So the tables differ. But some parts of these two labels are identical, and those are the parts most worth knowing.

visual.stock_query: two labels with matching highlighted box

scenes.narration: What do both labels say in exactly the same way?
Both carry the same boxed warning, the most prominent kind the FDA uses. In rats, tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumors.

visual.stock_query: label with bordered warning box, neutral

scenes.narration: It's unknown whether tirzepatide causes these tumors in humans, including a type called medullary thyroid carcinoma.

visual.stock_query: calm neutral mascot with question mark

scenes.narration: And both labels say not to use it if you or a family member has had medullary thyroid carcinoma, or if you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2.

items: Personal or family history of MTC

scenes.narration: Both also list warnings for pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, low blood sugar when used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney problems linked to dehydration, and serious allergic reactions.

items: Low blood sugar with insulin or sulfonylurea

scenes.retention_device: List visual for a fast scan; pays off the s14 signpost

scenes.narration: And both note that tirzepatide may make birth control pills less effective. If you use them, that's a conversation worth having with your prescriber.

If you have trouble breathing, or swelling of your face, lips or throat, call 911 in the US or Canada, 999 in the UK, or 000 in Australia right away. If you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Trouble breathing, swelling, or severe stomach pain that won't go away: get help right away. 911 US/Canada, 999 UK, 000 Australia.

items: Severe stomach pain that won't go away: get help right away

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

scenes.narration: And please don't switch between Mounjaro and Zepbound on your own either. Which brand fits you is a decision for you and your prescriber.
Now, that device I promised you at the start. This is the part of the label you can actually hold in your hand.
scenes.retention_device: Returns to the opening loop, raises anticipation

scenes.narration: So what does each one actually come in?
Device options are printed in two places in each label: Section 3, Dosage Forms and Strengths, and Section 16, How Supplied.
scenes.retention_device: Shows the viewer where to look

scenes.narration: Mounjaro's US label lists four: a single-dose pen, a single-dose vial, a multi-dose vial, and a KwikPen.
Zepbound's US label lists the same four: a single-dose pen, a single-dose vial, a multi-dose vial, and a KwikPen.

visual.stock_query: matching row of four cartoon devices

scenes.retention_device: Count reveal with a twist: they match

scenes.narration: That KwikPen is the one many people haven't heard of. It holds four doses and is for one person only, never shared.

visual.stat_label: KwikPen in both US labels, one person only
visual.stock_query: single pen with four small dots

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: So the loop closes like this: in the US, both labels list the same four device options. Your device can change, even when the medicine inside doesn't.
scenes.retention_device: Loop closed explicitly, opens the practical turn

scenes.narration: But here's the practical part. Each device has its own Instructions for Use, a separate leaflet with its own steps. Don't assume a pen's steps carry over to a vial or a KwikPen.
For example, the single-dose pen has its own leaflet, with pictured steps for that pen alone.
So if your device ever changes, ask your pharmacist or prescriber to walk you through that device's own Instructions for Use.
scenes.on_screen_text: New device? Ask for a walkthrough

scenes.narration: And if you're watching from outside the US, there's one more twist.
Is it the same story everywhere? Not quite.
In the European Union, for example, Mounjaro's authorisation covers both type 2 diabetes and weight management. So outside the US, check your own country's product information with your prescriber.

visual.stock_query: map of Europe with label icon

scenes.retention_device: Surprising contrast with the US label

scenes.narration: So what do you actually do with all of this?
Back to Dana. Nobody handed her the wrong thing. She and her brother take the same molecule, under two US labels, for different approved uses.

visual.stock_query: Dana smiling, relieved at kitchen table

scenes.retention_device: Last payoff of the thread before the recap

scenes.narration: And her worry turned into four good questions for her next appointment. Here they are.
One: which label am I on, and for which approved use?
Two: which device is mine, and have I read its own Instructions for Use?

items: Have I read its own leaflet?

scenes.narration: Three: do any of the label's warnings apply to me, like a thyroid history in my family?

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient reviewing a list

scenes.narration: Four: should any of my other medicines, including birth control pills, be reviewed?

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe. I checked it against the live Mounjaro and Zepbound US Prescribing Information (both revised 8/2026), the EMA EPAR for Mounjaro (updated 08/10/2026) and published summaries of SURPASS-1, SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-OSA. Everything below matches the sources:
- **Mounjaro indications:** blood sugar control in adults and children 10 and older, plus lowering major cardiovascular events in high-risk adults with type 2 diabetes. No weight use in the US label.
- **Zepbound indications:** weight management and moderate to severe sleep apnea, with the full populations. Its Limitations of Use say not to combine it with other tirzepatide products or GLP-1 medicines.
- **Devices:** both US labels list a single-dose pen, a single-dose vial, a 4-dose multi-dose vial and a 4-dose single-patient-use KwikPen.
- **Label numbers:** pancreatitis 0.23 vs 0.11 (Mounjaro diabetes pool) and 0.14 vs 0.15 (Zepbound weight trials). The wording on stomach side effects during dose escalation matches. Study 1 excluded diabetes and Study 2 enrolled only people with type 2 diabetes.
- **Shared warnings:** boxed-warning wording, the warnings list and the "may" hedge on birth control pills all match both labels.
- **Trials:** SURPASS-1 HbA1c −1.87 to −2.07 over 40 weeks. SURMOUNT-1 had 2,539 adults without diabetes, with −15.0% to −20.9% vs −3.1% at 72 weeks. SURMOUNT-OSA breathing events per hour fell −25.3 vs −5.3 (no machine) and −29.3 vs −5.5 (with machine) over 52 weeks.
- **EU:** Mounjaro is authorised for both type 2 diabetes and weight management.

The fixed safety lines, emergency line, don't-switch line, prescriber line and closing line are all present. Dana is clearly a made-up example.

PubMed pages served a cookie wall, so I confirmed S5, S6 and S7 through search results and published summaries. Their PMIDs and titles match. There are two minor wording fixes and nothing that blocks the video.

issues.claim: Over 72 weeks, average weight change on tirzepatide ranged from about 15 to 21 percent, depending on dose. On placebo, it was three point one percent.
issues.problem: Spoken without a minus sign or the word 'loss', 'weight change … 15 to 21 percent' and 'three point one percent' could be heard as weight gain. The on-screen text uses minus signs, so muted and listening viewers get different wording.
issues.fix: Over 72 weeks, average weight loss on tirzepatide ranged from about 15 to 21 percent, depending on dose. On placebo, the average loss was three point one percent.

issues.claim: In Zepbound's weight trials, it was zero point one four on tirzepatide, versus zero point one five on placebo.
issues.problem: The figure is correct and correctly scoped. But the Zepbound label also reports 0.84 vs 0 per 100 years in the sleep apnea trials (Studies 5 and 6). Leaving that out makes the label's pancreatitis picture look more reassuring than it is. This is optional for transparency, not an error.
issues.fix: Optional: add to s40 narration: "In its sleep apnea trials, the label lists zero point eight four on tirzepatide, versus zero on placebo." Add a matching on-screen pill: "Zepbound sleep apnea trials: 0.84 vs 0 per 100 years". If you skip this, keep s40 exactly as written, scoped to 'weight trials'.
